Error Establishing a Database Connection: What It Means and How to Fix It

By WevTEC Review TeamPublished Jun 12, 2021Updated Oct 25, 202612 min read
On This Page
  1. The short answer
  2. What the error means
  3. The four usual causes
  4. Check wp-config.php
  5. Is the server up?
  6. Repairing a corrupted table
  7. When it follows a change
  8. When it means a hack
  9. Preventing a repeat
  10. Questions people ask AI
  11. How WevTEC Fix Website Issues helps

Site still down? Book a free consultation

Your site was fine this morning. Now every page — including the login screen — shows one line of text on a white background: Error establishing a database connection. No menu, no theme, no way in.

It looks catastrophic and usually isn’t. Here is what the message means, the four causes behind nearly every case, how to check each without making things worse, and when carrying on alone starts to risk real damage.

The short answer

WordPress stores your content in a database and reads it on every page load. This error means that connection failed. Four causes cover almost all cases: wrong credentials in wp-config.php, a database server that is down or out of connections, a corrupted table, or a full disk.

Start by comparing the database name, user, password and host in wp-config.php against your hosting panel — a mismatch here is the single most common cause, especially after a migration or a password change. Then check your disk usage and open phpMyAdmin to confirm the database server is responding.

Your content is almost certainly intact, so do not restore an old backup until you know what failed.

What the error actually means

The message is literal. WordPress is a PHP application that keeps almost everything — your posts, pages, users, settings, widget configuration, WooCommerce orders — in a MySQL or MariaDB database. The files on your server are only the program. The words on your site live in the database.

On every page load, WordPress reads the connection details from wp-config.php and queries the database. If that connection fails, there is nothing to render, so WordPress prints this one line instead. That is why the front end and /wp-admin go down together.

The four causes, in the order worth checking

In practice, nearly every case comes down to one of four things. Work through them in this order, because the list runs from most common and safest to least common and riskiest.

  1. Wrong credentials in wp-config.php. The database name, user, password or host doesn’t match what the server expects. Typical after a migration, a host account change, or a password reset in cPanel.
  2. The database server is down or refusing connections. Shared hosting hits connection limits under load; a MySQL service can crash or be stopped during maintenance.
  3. A corrupted table. Less common than the internet suggests, but real, usually after an unclean shutdown, a disk-full event or an interrupted import.
  4. Something changed. A plugin or theme update, a disk quota that filled up, or an intrusion that rewrote your configuration file.

One quick test tells you a lot. If the front end shows the error but /wp-admin shows “One or more database tables are unavailable. The database may need to be repaired,” you are looking at corruption rather than bad credentials. If both show the identical plain error, start with credentials and server availability.

Start here: check wp-config.php

Open wp-config.php in the root of your WordPress install, using your host’s File Manager or SFTP. Download a copy before you touch it. Four lines matter:

define( 'DB_NAME', 'your_database_name' );
define( 'DB_USER', 'your_database_user' );
define( 'DB_PASSWORD', 'your_password' );
define( 'DB_HOST', 'localhost' );

Compare each one against what your hosting panel reports under MySQL Databases. Three details trip people up repeatedly:

  • Prefixes. Most shared hosts prepend your account name, so the database you created as wpsite is really cpanelusr_wpsite, and the user you created as wpuser is really cpanelusr_wpuser. The short version will never connect.
  • The user is not attached to the database. Creating a user is a separate step from granting it access. In cPanel this is “Add User to Database,” and the user needs All Privileges.
  • DB_HOST is not always localhost. Many managed and cloud hosts use a dedicated hostname such as mysql.yourhost.com or an address with a port. Your host’s documentation states the correct value.

If you reset the database user’s password in the hosting panel to be sure, you must paste that same password into wp-config.php. Changing it in one place and not the other is one of the most common ways this error appears out of nowhere.

Edit with a plain text editor, never Word or Google Docs: a smart quote or a space before <?php will break the file. The wp-config.php reference documents every constant it accepts.

Is the database server actually up?

If the credentials are provably correct, the next question is whether the database server is answering at all. Two checks settle it.

Open phpMyAdmin from your hosting panel. If phpMyAdmin itself errors or hangs, the problem is the server, not your site, and no amount of editing wp-config.php will help. If phpMyAdmin opens and your tables are listed with sensible row counts, the server is healthy and the data is intact.

Check your disk quota. A full account is a frequent and badly signposted cause. MySQL cannot write temporary files when the disk is full, so connections start failing. Hosting panels show disk usage on the main dashboard; if you are at 100%, clear old backups, large logs or stale media before anything else.

On shared hosting, too many simultaneous connections can also exhaust the limit your plan allows — from a traffic spike, a bot crawl, or a plugin querying in a loop. The symptom is distinctive: the site fails under load and recovers when things go quiet. That is a capacity conversation with your host.

Repairing a corrupted database, carefully

Only do this if /wp-admin showed “database may need to be repaired,” or phpMyAdmin reports crashed tables. Repair writes to your tables, so export a copy from phpMyAdmin first.

WordPress includes a repair tool that is switched off by default. Add this line to wp-config.php, above the line that says “That’s all, stop editing”:

define( 'WP_ALLOW_REPAIR', true );

Then visit https://yoursite.com/wp-admin/maint/repair.php. You will be offered “Repair Database” and “Repair and Optimize Database.” Choose repair alone first; optimize takes considerably longer on a large site and is not needed to fix the error.

Remove that line as soon as you are finished. While it is present the repair page is reachable by anyone, without logging in. Leaving it in place is a genuine security hole, and the WordPress documentation says the same.

If repair reports success but the error persists, or tables will not repair, the damage is deeper than this tool handles. That is the point to restore a recent database backup or get someone experienced involved, rather than running more repair attempts.

When it appears right after a change

If the site was working an hour ago, something changed. Narrowing down what changed is faster than general troubleshooting.

After a migration or host move. Almost always the credentials. The new host issues a new database name, user and password, and the copied wp-config.php still points at the old ones. Check DB_HOST especially, since it rarely matches between providers.

After a plugin or theme update. A plugin cannot normally break the database connection, but a failed update can leave the site mid-write with a full disk or a locked table. Check disk space, then look at your error log before blaming the plugin.

After a password change. Resetting the MySQL user password in the hosting panel does not update wp-config.php. The two must match.

Logging beats guesswork. Set WP_DEBUG and WP_DEBUG_LOG as described in Debugging in WordPress, reproduce the error, then read wp-content/debug.log. Keep WP_DEBUG_DISPLAY off so visitors never see it, and switch debugging off afterwards.

When the error is a symptom of something worse

Occasionally this error is a side effect of an intrusion. The pattern: it appears with no change you made, wp-config.php has a modification date you cannot explain, or the credentials in it were altered to values that were never yours.

Compromised sites also accumulate junk — thousands of spam posts or injected rows — until queries time out. If you find unfamiliar admin users, posts you did not write, or redirects to unrelated sites once access is restored, treat it as a security incident, not a database fault. Our guide to WordPress malware removal plugins covers scanning, and hacked website repair is the service side.

Restoring a backup over a compromised site without finding how the attacker got in usually means the same problem returns within days.

Keeping it from happening again

Most repeat occurrences are preventable with a few habits:

  • Keep a current backup of files and database, stored somewhere other than the server itself. WordPress’s backup documentation covers the options. A backup you have never restored is a guess, so test one occasionally.
  • Save a copy of wp-config.php before any migration or host change. It takes a second and removes the worst part of the problem.
  • Watch disk usage. Set an alert at 80% rather than discovering the problem when the site stops.
  • Keep PHP current. Old versions lose security support and eventually conflict with the database drivers your host upgrades. The PHP supported versions page shows what is still maintained.

Questions people ask AI about this error

“What does “error establishing a database connection” actually mean?”

WordPress could not reach the database that stores your content. The files are fine and the data usually is too; only the connection failed. Common causes are wrong credentials in wp-config.php, a database server that is down or at its connection limit, a corrupted table, or a full disk.

“Did I lose my website content?”

Almost certainly not. The error is about reaching the database, not the data inside it. Open phpMyAdmin from your hosting panel: if your tables are there with normal row counts, your content is intact. Do not restore an old backup until you know the cause.

“Can I fix this myself without a developer?”

Often, yes. Checking the four credentials in wp-config.php against your hosting panel, and checking your disk space, solves most cases and needs no coding. Get help if the database server itself is failing, if tables will not repair, or if you suspect a hack.

“Why did this happen suddenly when I changed nothing?”

Something usually changed on the server: the disk filled up, a database password was rotated, the host moved your account, or traffic exhausted your connection limit. Errors that come and go with traffic point to connection limits; errors at the same time each day point to a scheduled job.

“Will this error hurt my Google rankings?”

A short outage normally does not, because Google retries. The risk grows if the site is down for days, since repeated failures can reduce crawl frequency and eventually affect indexing. Fix it promptly and you should see no lasting effect.

“How much does it cost to fix a database connection error?”

It depends on the cause. A credentials mismatch is quick; a corrupted database, a hacked site or a failed migration takes longer. Our website repairs start at $50, and we confirm the cause and the price before any work begins.
